claim: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is characterized by demyelinated and inflammatory lesions in the brain and spinal cord that are highly variable in terms of cellular content.
source: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is characterized by demyelinated and inflammatory lesions in the brain and spinal cord that are highly variable in terms of cellular content.
evidence: This is a general statement about MS pathology that is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) enables the simultaneous imaging of 15+ proteins within staged MS lesions.
source: Here, we used imaging mass cytometry (IMC) to enable the simultaneous imaging of 15+ proteins within staged MS lesions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the application of IMC technology to MS tissue with a panel of 15+ antibodies.

claim: IMC can discriminate demyelinating macrophages from the resident microglial pool.
source: With post-acquisition analysis pipelines we were able to: (1) Discriminate demyelinating macrophages from the resident microglial pool
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing differentiation of macrophages from microglia using specific markers.

claim: IMC can determine which types of lymphocytes reside closest to blood vessels.
source: (2) Determine which types of lymphocytes reside closest to blood vessels
evidence: Distance analysis from blood vessels was performed for different lymphocyte populations.

claim: IMC can identify multiple subsets of T and B cells.
source: (3) Identify multiple subsets of T and B cells
evidence: The manuscript demonstrates identification of various T and B cell subsets using multiple markers.

claim: IMC can ascertain dynamics of T cell phenotypes vis-à-vis lesion type and location.
source: (4) Ascertain dynamics of T cell phenotypes vis-à-vis lesion type and location.
evidence: T cell phenotypes were analyzed across different lesion types and locations.

claim: MS is a disease with profound heterogeneity in the neuropathological and immunopathological appearance of lesions in the central nervous system (CNS).
source: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a disease with profound heterogeneity in the neuropathological and immunopathological appearance of lesions in the central nervous system (CNS) (Lucchinetti et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lucchinetti et al., 2000.

claim: Recent consensus has standardized staging of MS brain tissue into categories including normal-appearing white matter (NAWM), (p)reactive lesions, periplaque white matter (PPWM), early or late active demyelinating lesions, mixed active/inactive demyelinating lesions, and inactive lesions.
source: Recent consensus has standardized staging of MS brain tissue into categories including normal-appearing white matter (NAWM), (p)reactive lesions (or 'pre-phagocytic' lesions) (Barnett and Prineas, 2004) which may represent an initial lesion (Marik et al., 2007; Alvarez et al., 2015), periplaque white matter (PPWM) which is immediately adjacent to a lesion, early or late active demyelinating lesions, mixed active/inactive demyelinating lesions (also called slowly expanding or 'smouldering'; see Frischer et al., 2015), and inactive lesions (Kuhlmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing lesion staging consensus.

claim: (P)reactive lesions may represent an initial lesion.
source: (p)reactive lesions (or 'pre-phagocytic' lesions) (Barnett and Prineas, 2004) which may represent an initial lesion (Marik et al., 2007; Alvarez et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Marik et al., 2007 and Alvarez et al., 2015.

claim: Pattern I demyelination is T cell-mediated.
source: with pattern I being T cell-mediated
evidence: This is part of the description of demyelination patterns from Lucchinetti et al., 2000.

claim: Pattern II demyelination is IgG- and complement-mediated.
source: pattern II being IgG- and complement-mediated
evidence: This is part of the description of demyelination patterns from Lucchinetti et al., 2000.

claim: Pattern III and IV demyelination are characterized by a primary oligodendrocyte dystrophy reminiscent of virus- or toxin-induced demyelination rather than autoimmunity.
source: pattern III and IV characterized by a primary oligodendrocyte dystrophy reminiscent of virus- or toxin-induced demyelination rather than autoimmunity (Lucchinetti et al., 2000).
evidence: This is part of the description of demyelination patterns from Lucchinetti et al., 2000.

claim: Lymphocytes, microglia and macrophages are associated with active demyelination and neurodegeneration in the MS brain.
source: Lymphocytes, microglia and macrophages are associated with active demyelination and neurodegeneration in the MS brain (Frischer et al., 2009; Haider et al., 2014)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Frischer et al., 2009 and Haider et al., 2014.

claim: Lymphocytes, microglia and macrophages are thought to play key roles in the MS disease process, as supported by studies in experimental models.
source: and are thought to play key roles in the disease process, as supported by studies in experimental models (reviewed in Robinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review by Robinson et al., 2014.

claim: Yolk sac-derived (resident) microglia and blood-derived (recruited) monocytes/macrophages accumulate at sites of active demyelination and neuroaxonal injury.
source: With respect to myeloid cells, yolk sac-derived (resident) microglia and blood-derived (recruited) monocytes/macrophages accumulate at sites of active demyelination and neuroaxonal injury (Frischer et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Frischer et al., 2009.

claim: Microglia and macrophages within the MS brain can lose their normally homeostatic properties and acquire a pro-inflammatory phenotype with expression of molecules involved in phagocytosis, oxidative injury, antigen presentation and T cell co-stimulation.
source: Microglia and macrophages within the MS brain can lose their normally homeostatic properties and acquire a pro-inflammatory phenotype with expression of molecules involved in phagocytosis, oxidative injury, antigen presentation and T cell co-stimulation (Gay et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gay et al., 1997.

claim: T cell-mediated recognition of myelin epitopes can initiate a process that results in the activation of microglia and recruitment of macrophages at the lesion site.
source: Either via T cell-mediated recognition of myelin epitopes (Sun et al., 2001) or complement binding to myelin autoantibodies (Storch et al., 1998), these lymphocyte-dependent events initiate a process that results in the activation of microglia and recruitment of macrophages at the lesion site.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sun et al., 2001 and Storch et al., 1998.

claim: Complement binding to myelin autoantibodies can initiate a process that results in the activation of microglia and recruitment of macrophages at the lesion site.
source: Either via T cell-mediated recognition of myelin epitopes (Sun et al., 2001) or complement binding to myelin autoantibodies (Storch et al., 1998), these lymphocyte-dependent events initiate a process that results in the activation of microglia and recruitment of macrophages at the lesion site.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sun et al., 2001 and Storch et al., 1998.

claim: The detection of small (myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, MOG) or large (proteolipid protein, PLP) myelin proteins indicates the temporal development of myelin destruction.
source: The detection of small (myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, MOG) or large (proteolipid protein, PLP) myelin proteins indicates the temporal development of myelin destruction (Lucchinetti et al., 2000; Kuhlmann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lucchinetti et al., 2000 and Kuhlmann et al., 2017.

claim: MS lesions contain T cells and CD20+ B cells.
source: In terms of lymphocytes, MS lesions contain T cells and CD20+ B cells (Machado-Santos et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Machado-Santos et al., 2018.

claim: In active lesions, CD8+ T cells proliferate and have an activated cytotoxic phenotype.
source: In active lesions, CD8+ T cells proliferate and have an activated cytotoxic phenotype.
evidence: This is a statement about CD8+ T cell behavior in active lesions, supported by the context of the manuscript.

claim: Some CD8+ T cells are destroyed by apoptosis while others, with tissue-resident memory features, persist.
source: Subsequently, some CD8+ T cells are destroyed by apoptosis while others, with tissue-resident memory features, persist.
evidence: This describes the fate of CD8+ T cells in MS lesions.

claim: Tissue resident memory T cells lose expression of surface molecules that are involved in the egress of leukocytes from inflamed tissue, which has been suggested as a potential mechanism responsible for the compartmentalized inflammatory response in established lesions.
source: Tissue resident memory T cells lose expression of surface molecules that are involved in the egress of leukocytes from inflamed tissue, which has been suggested as a potential mechanism responsible for the compartmentalized inflammatory response in established lesions (Machado-Santos et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Machado-Santos et al., 2018.

claim: CD4+ T cells are found in MS lesions and have been shown to produce cytokines such as IL-17 and IFNγ.
source: CD4+ T cells are also found in MS lesions and have been shown to produce cytokines such as IL-17 and IFNγ (Kebir et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kebir et al., 2007.

claim: B cells are thought to differentiate into plasma cells, perhaps in situ, but little is known about their phenotype.
source: B cells are thought to differentiate into plasma cells, perhaps in situ, but little is known about their phenotype (Machado-Santos et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Machado-Santos et al., 2018.

claim: Past and recent immunohistological studies have provided insights into the types of immune cells populating MS lesions at different lesional stages and the neurodegenerative changes that accompany these infiltrating immune cells.
source: While past and recent immunohistological studies have provided insights into the types of immune cells populating MS lesions at different lesional stages and the neurodegenerative changes that accompany these infiltrating immune cells (Frischer et al., 2009; Machado-Santos et al., 2018; Luchetti et al., 2018; Zrzavy et al., 2017; Popescu et al., 2017; Fischer et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Immunohistological analysis requires immunohistological staining of serial sections and is limited to the number of analytes that can be simultaneously visualized on a given tissue section.
source: this type of analysis requires immunohistological staining of serial sections and is limited to the number of analytes that can be simultaneously visualized on a given tissue section.
evidence: This is a known limitation of traditional immunohistology.

claim: A comprehensive analysis of single-cell phenotypes and functional states in relation to demyelination within MS tissue is lacking.
source: Thus, a comprehensive analysis of single-cell phenotypes and functional states in relation to demyelination within MS tissue is lacking.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the field that the current study addresses.

claim: IMC uses time-of-flight inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry to detect dozens of markers simultaneously on a single tissue section.
source: IMC uses time-of-flight inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry to detect dozens of markers simultaneously on a single tissue section.
evidence: This describes the technical basis of IMC.

claim: IMC achieves multiplexed detection by measuring the abundance of metal isotopes tagged to antibodies and indexed against their source location.
source: It achieves this by measuring the abundance of metal isotopes tagged to antibodies and indexed against their source location (Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chang et al., 2017.

claim: The study analyzed staged lesions in a case with severe rebound MS disease activity after natalizumab (NTZ) cessation.
source: Applying this new technology to post-mortem MS brain tissue, we carefully analysed staged lesions in a case with severe rebound MS disease activity after natalizumab (NTZ, also known as anti-VLA4) cessation (Larochelle et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the specific case studied, supported by a citation to Larochelle et al., 2017.

claim: The highly inflammatory nature of the lesions present in the brain of the NTZ rebound case makes this tissue a good positive control to test a variety of analytes involved in neuroinflammation.
source: The highly inflammatory nature of the lesions present in the brain of this specific case, makes this tissue a good positive control to test a variety of analytes involved in neuroinflammation.
evidence: This is a rationale for using this particular case.

claim: IMC, in combination with existing imaging techniques, can profoundly impact knowledge of the inflammatory response and tissue injury in the MS brain.
source: The data we collected suggest that IMC, in combination with existing imaging techniques, can profoundly impact our knowledge of the inflammatory response and tissue injury in the MS brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Two separate IMC runs were performed on the same patient and control tissue.
source: In this study, we performed two separate IMC runs on the same patient and control tissue.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: The first IMC run was to validate the panel and the approach in general.
source: The first run (Figures 1–2) was to validate our panel and the approach in general.
evidence: This describes the purpose of the first IMC run.

claim: The second IMC run was to evaluate the composition of immune cells across several types of lesions and sub-lesional areas.
source: The second run (Figures 3–7) was to evaluate the composition of immune cells across several types of lesions and sub-lesional areas.
evidence: This describes the purpose of the second IMC run.

claim: Imaging of equivalent ROI in IF- and IMC-stained sections showed similar staining patterns with clearly resolved anatomical regions.
source: Imaging of equivalent ROI in IF- and IMC-stained sections showed similar staining patterns with clearly resolved anatomical regions (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: IMC is able to resolve myelin engulfed by microglia/macrophages with a similar pattern as what is observed using IHC and IF approaches.
source: We also showed that IMC is able to resolve myelin engulfed by microglia/macrophages with a similar pattern as what is observed using IHC and IF approaches (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

source: All comparisons yielded a significant positive correlation (Spearman correlation coefficient: r = 0.9182, p=0.0002; r = 0.8929, p=0.01; r = 0.9544, p<0.0001; r = 0.9794, p<0.0001; r = 0.9051, p<0.0001 for nuclei, CD3+ T cells, %PLP+ area, HLA+ cells and CD68+ cells respectively)

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between the number of CD3+ T cells identified with FITC-labeled secondary antibody by IF and the number of CD3+ T cells identified with the 170Er metal-tag by IMC (Spearman correlation coefficient: r = 0.8929, p=0.01).
source: All comparisons yielded a significant positive correlation (Spearman correlation coefficient: r = 0.9182, p=0.0002; r = 0.8929, p=0.01; r = 0.9544, p<0.0001; r = 0.9794, p<0.0001; r = 0.9051, p<0.0001 for nuclei, CD3+ T cells, %PLP+ area, HLA+ cells and CD68+ cells respectively)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1c.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between the % of PLP+ area identified with AF568-labeled secondary antibody by IF and % of PLP+ area identified with the 141Pr metal-tag by IMC (Spearman correlation coefficient: r = 0.9544, p<0.0001).
source: All comparisons yielded a significant positive correlation (Spearman correlation coefficient: r = 0.9182, p=0.0002; r = 0.8929, p=0.01; r = 0.9544, p<0.0001; r = 0.9794, p<0.0001; r = 0.9051, p<0.0001 for nuclei, CD3+ T cells, %PLP+ area, HLA+ cells and CD68+ cells respectively)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4a.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between the number of HLA+ myeloid cells identified with FITC-labeled secondary antibody by IF and the number of HLA+ myeloid cells identified with the 147Sm metal-tag by IMC (Spearman correlation coefficient: r = 0.9794, p<0.0001).
source: All comparisons yielded a significant positive correlation (Spearman correlation coefficient: r = 0.9182, p=0.0002; r = 0.8929, p=0.01; r = 0.9544, p<0.0001; r = 0.9794, p<0.0001; r = 0.9051, p<0.0001 for nuclei, CD3+ T cells, %PLP+ area, HLA+ cells and CD68+ cells respectively)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4b.

claim: There is a significant positive correlation between the number of CD68+ myeloid cells identified with FITC-labeled secondary antibody by IF and the number of CD68+ myeloid cells identified with the 159Tb metal-tag by IMC (Spearman correlation coefficient: r = 0.9051, p<0.0001).
source: All comparisons yielded a significant positive correlation (Spearman correlation coefficient: r = 0.9182, p=0.0002; r = 0.8929, p=0.01; r = 0.9544, p<0.0001; r = 0.9794, p<0.0001; r = 0.9051, p<0.0001 for nuclei, CD3+ T cells, %PLP+ area, HLA+ cells and CD68+ cells respectively)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4c.

claim: IMC reproduces staining patterns that are in agreement with those produced using the more standard IF method in an NTZ-rebound brain tissue.
source: In summary, IMC reproduces staining patterns that are in agreement with those produced using the more standard IF method in an NTZ-rebound brain tissue.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analyses.

claim: IMC imaging of the edge of an active demyelinating lesion identified CD3+CD45+ T cells and CD3-CD45+ leukocytes other than T cells.
source: IMC imaging of the edge of an active demyelinating lesion identified CD3+CD45+ T cells and CD3-CD45+ leukocytes other than T cells (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The co-expression of CD68 in CD3-CD45+ cells identifies these as microglia/macrophages (CD3-CD45+CD68+).
source: The co-expression of CD68 in CD3-CD45+ cells identifies these as microglia/macrophages (CD3-CD45+CD68+) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: CD3+ T cells lack expression of immunoglobulin light chain, (CD3+κ/λ-).
source: As expected, CD3+ T cells lack expression of immunoglobulin light chain, (CD3+κ/λ-).
evidence: This is an expected finding based on known biology of T cells.

claim: B cells were identified that were either positive for the κ or λ light chain and negative for the CD3 marker of T cells and the CD68 marker of macrophages.
source: Moreover, we identified B cells that were either positive for the κ or λ light chain and negative for the CD3 marker of T cells and the CD68 marker of macrophages (for example, CD3-CD68-κ+ B cells in Figure 2c arrow, versus CD3-CD68-λ- B cells in Figure 2d arrow and vice versa CD3-CD68-κ- B cells in Figure 2c arrow head, versus CD3-CD68-λ+ B cells in Figure 2d arrow head).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2c and 2d.

claim: The extracellular matrix protein collagen (not cell-associated) surrounded putative blood vessels lined by endothelial cells that expressed the CD31 marker as expected.
source: We found that the extracellular matrix protein collagen (not cell-associated) surrounded putative blood vessels lined by endothelial cells that expressed the CD31 marker as expected.
evidence: This is an expected finding based on known biology of blood vessels.

claim: Macrophages visualized by CD68 do not stain positive for collagen nor express CD31 (CD31-collagen-CD68+).
source: In contrast, macrophages visualized by CD68 do not stain positive for collagen nor express CD31 (CD31-collagen-CD68+) (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: IMC identified a granzyme B+ signal with granular expression in close proximity to nuclei.
source: IMC identified a granzyme B+ signal with granular expression in close proximity to nuclei (Figure 2f,g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2f and 2g.

claim: IMC enables imaging of multiple markers on a single tissue section reproducing IF-equivalent staining patterns and with cell lineage-specific markers expressed on appropriate cell types.
source: These results show that IMC enables imaging of multiple markers on a single tissue section reproducing IF-equivalent staining patterns and with cell lineage-specific markers expressed on appropriate cell types.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation experiments.

claim: Control white matter showed intact myelin staining with few HLA+ cells.
source: Consistent with the generally non-inflamed and myelinated state of healthy white matter, control white matter showed intact myelin staining with few HLA+ cells (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3a and 3b.

claim: Normal appearing white matter (NAWM) in the NTZ rebound brain exhibited normal myelin staining, however HLA+ cells within the NTZ rebound NAWM appeared enriched when compared to control white matter.
source: Normal appearing white matter (NAWM) in the NTZ rebound brain exhibited normal myelin staining, however HLA+ cells within the NTZ rebound NAWM appeared enriched when compared to control white matter (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: The (p)reactive lesion showed a normal myelin signal but HLA+ cells accumulated at this site.
source: Similarly, the (p)reactive lesion showed a normal myelin signal but HLA+ cells accumulated at this site (Figure 3e,f).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3e and 3f.

claim: The active lesion core showed loss of PLP signal with accumulation of HLA+ cells.
source: The active lesion core showed loss of PLP signal with accumulation of HLA+ cells (Figure 3g,h).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3g and 3h.

claim: The mixed active-inactive lesions showed reduced myelin and accumulation of HLA+ cells at the lesion edge.
source: The mixed active-inactive lesions showed reduced myelin and accumulation of HLA+ cells at the lesion edge (Figure 3i,j).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3i and 3j.

claim: HLA+ cells that contained PLP myelin products were found in both active lesions and at the edge of mixed active-inactive lesions, indicative of demyelinating activity.
source: HLA+ cells that contained PLP myelin products were found in both active lesions (Larochelle et al., 2017) (Figure 3k) and at the edge of mixed active-inactive lesions (Figure 3l), indicative of demyelinating activity.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3k and 3l.

claim: Application of IMC to different ROI was able to differentiate between normal-appearing tissue and different lesional stages of the NTZ rebound brain.
source: Collectively we were able to show that application of IMC to different ROI (pre-selected on the bases of PLP/HLA IF staining on a serial section) was able to differentiate between normal-appearing tissue and different lesional stages of the NTZ rebound brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of different lesion types.

claim: In the white matter from a control subject, microglia identified as being TMEM119+ generally showed a thin ramified morphology, typical of resting cells.
source: In the white matter from a control subject we found that microglia, identified as being TMEM119+21, generally showed a thin ramified morphology, typical of resting cells (Figure 4a,a' dotted arrows).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4a,a'.

claim: On resting microglia, the HLA marker of antigen presentation was generally low or not detectable, confirming a quiescent state.
source: On these cells, the HLA marker of antigen presentation was generally low or not detectable, confirming a quiescent state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HLA expression data on TMEM119+ cells.

claim: TMEM119+ microglia that showed a more rounded morphology, a sign of activation, also stained positive for HLA and CD68 which is indicative of antigen presentation and phagocytic activity, respectively.
source: On the contrary, TMEM119+ microglia that showed a more rounded morphology, a sign of activation, also stained positive for HLA and CD68 which is indicative of antigen presentation and phagocytic activity, respectively (Figure 4a,a' arrow head and b, b' arrow head).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4a,a' and 4b,b'.

claim: TMEM119-HLA+CD68+ cells were identified as macrophages and were present in the white matter of a control.
source: TMEM119-HLA+CD68+ cells were identified as macrophages and were also present in the white matter of a control (Figure 4a,a' arrow and b, b' arrow).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4a,a' and 4b,b'.

claim: In the normal white matter of a control subject some microglia (TMEM119+) and some macrophages (TMEM119-) have an activated phenotype (HLA+CD68+).
source: These data indicate that in the normal white matter of a control subject some microglia (TMEM119+) and some macrophages (TMEM119-) have an activated phenotype (HLA+CD68+).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of control white matter.

claim: Visualization of the expression pattern of microglia and macrophage markers in the normal-appearing white matter showed some TMEM119+ microglia with ramified morphology, similar to control white matter.
source: Visualization of the expression pattern of microglia and macrophage markers in the normal-appearing white matter showed some TMEM119+ microglia with ramified morphology (Figure 4c,c' dotted arrows), similar to control white matter.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4c,c'.

claim: Unlike control white matter, the normal-appearing white matter showed many TMEM119+ microglia that were also positive for HLA and CD68.
source: However unlike control white matter, the normal-appearing white matter showed many TMEM119+ microglia that were also positive for HLA and CD68 (Figure 4c,c' arrows head and d, d' arrows head).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4c,c' and 4d,d'.

claim: A few TMEM119-HLA+CD68+ macrophages were present in the normal-appearing tissue.
source: A few TMEM119-HLA+CD68+ macrophages were also present in the normal-appearing tissue (Figure 4c,c' arrow and d, d' arrow).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4c,c' and 4d,d'.

claim: Within the (p)reactive lesions, TMEM119+ microglia accumulated, showed an enlarged morphology that is indicative of an activated state, and expressed both HLA and CD68.
source: Within the (p)reactive lesions, TMEM119+ microglia accumulated, showed an enlarged morphology that is indicative of an activated state, and expressed both HLA and CD68 (Figure 4e,e' and e'' arrows head and f, f' arrows head).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4e,e', e'' and 4f,f'.

claim: TMEM119-HLA+CD68+ macrophages were present in (p)reactive lesions.
source: TMEM119-HLA+CD68+ macrophages were also present (Figure 4e,e' arrows and f, f' arrows).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4e,e' and 4f,f'.

claim: Active lesions contained high numbers of TMEM119+HLA+CD68+ microglia and TMEM119-HLA+CD68+ macrophages, most of them with enlarged and foamy morphology that is typical of the activated and phagocytic state.
source: Active lesions contained high numbers of TMEM119+HLA+CD68+ microglia and TMEM119-HLA+CD68+ macrophages, most of them with enlarged and foamy morphology that is typical of the activated and phagocytic state (Figure 4g,g' and g'' arrows and h, h' arrows).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4g,g', g'' and 4h,h'.

claim: The edge of mixed active-inactive lesions was characterized by a rim of dense TMEM119+HLA+ microglia and TMEM119-HLA+ macrophages, both with obvious enlarged CD68+ lysosomes.
source: The edge of these lesions was characterized by a rim of dense TMEM119+HLA+ microglia (Figure 4i,i' arrow head and j, j' arrow head) and TMEM119-HLA+ macrophages (Figure 4i,i' arrows and j, j', j'' arrows), both with obvious enlarged CD68+ lysosomes (Figure 4j'' arrows).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4i,i', 4j,j', and 4j''.

claim: Only a few HLA+CD68+ cells were present in the inactive lesion core and microglia showed profound reduction in the HLA signal.
source: Only a few HLA+CD68+ cells were present in the inactive lesion core and microglia showed profound reduction in the HLA signal (Figure 4i,i' arrows and j, j', j'' arrows).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4i,i', 4j,j', and 4j''.

claim: In the white matter from a control subject CD3+CD8α- T cells or CD3+CD8α+ T cells were rare or absent.
source: In the white matter from a control subject CD3+CD8α- T cells or CD3+CD8α+ T cells were rare of absent (Figure 5a,a' and b,b').
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5a,a' and 5b,b'.

claim: In the normal-appearing white matter, some CD3+CD8α- T cells and some CD3+CD8α+ T cells were identified that did not show signs of activation as defined by the expression of NFAT1.
source: In the normal-appearing white matter, we identified some CD3+CD8α- T cells (Figure 5c,c' arrow) and some CD3+CD8α+ T cells (Figure 5c,c' dotted arrow) that did not show signs of activation as defined by the expression of NFAT1 which translocates to the nucleus of T cells upon T cell receptor activation (Ma et al., 2015) (Figure 5d,d' arrow and dotted arrow).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5c,c' and 5d,d', with citation to Ma et al., 2015.

claim: NFAT1 translocates to the nucleus of T cells upon T cell receptor activation.
source: that did not show signs of activation as defined by the expression of NFAT1 which translocates to the nucleus of T cells upon T cell receptor activation (Ma et al., 2015)
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2015.

claim: Within the (p)reactive lesions, CD3+CD8α- and CD3+CD8α+ T cells were both prominent but did not stain for NFAT1 and were therefore presumably not activated.
source: Within the (p)reactive lesions, CD3+CD8α- and CD3+CD8α+ T cells were both prominent (Figure 5e,e' arrow and dotted arrow, respectively) but did not stain for NFAT1 and were therefore presumably not activated (Figure 5f,f' arrow and dotted arrow, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5e,e' and 5f,f'.

claim: Active lesions contained both CD3+CD8α- and CD3+CD8α+ T cells, mostly located in the perivascular area, but also scattered in the parenchyma.
source: Active lesions contained both, CD3+CD8α- and CD3+CD8α+ T cells (Figure 5g,g' arrow and dotted arrow, respectively), mostly located in the perivascular area (Figure 5g' inset), but also scattered in the parenchyma.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5g and 5g'.

claim: Some CD3+CD8α+ T cells in active lesions were activated based on the expression of NFAT1.
source: Some CD3+CD8α+ T cells were also activated based on the expression of NFAT1 (Figure 5h,h' arrow head).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5h,h'.

claim: The edge of the slowly expanding lesions contained both CD3+CD8α- and CD3+CD8α+ T cells.
source: Similar to the core of active lesions, the edge of the slowly expanding lesions contained both, CD3+CD8α- and CD3+CD8α+ T cells (Figure 5i,i' arrow and dotted arrow, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5i,i'.

claim: A few CD3+CD8α- T cells and some CD3+CD8α+ T cells at the edge of slowly expanding lesions were NFAT1+.
